newsitem.title: UK: World oil markets slide gently as spring rally ends.
newsitem.headline: World oil markets slide gently as spring rally ends.

text.p: World oil prices slid gently lower on Friday after a week that saw some of the steam go out of crude's spring bull run.
Benchmark Brent crude oil futures for July delivery were trading quietly just eight cents down at $19.40 a barrel at 1500 gmt, 60 cents lower than last Friday's close.
In New York, NYMEX crude oil was down two cents on the day at $20.95, 58 cents softer on the week. Both markets were trading quietly with little news to stop them sagging.
The week's big fall came on Tuesday when investment funds joined a wholesale sell-off in the paper market, sparked by a report showing the market full to the limit with long positions.

Technical factors have since helped crude to recover a little but brokers believe most worries over short oil supplies have begun to dissipate, with the market facing a return to the bearish mood of the early part of the year.

Brent prices fell to a one year low of less than $18 in April before recovering to above the $20 mark as traders worried about tight North Sea supply and the renewal of Iraq's $2 billion oil-for-food agreement.
Traders said oil markets had now digested most of the bad news, although continued poor non-OPEC supply growth was a supportive factor.
For the second year running analysts have cut their forecasts for non-OPEC supply growth because new North Sea fields have failed to come on stream when planned.

"It's been a case in the North Sea of a lot of new technology and really aggressive timescales which have not been realistic enough," said Steve Scullion of Edinburgh-based consultants Wood Mackenzie.
Market pundits reckon there will be a shortfall of 300,000 barrels per day, easing the downward price pressure on OPEC oil, which has been under threat because of the cartel's own over-production.
Most traders assume the United Nations will renew the deal allowing Iraq to export oil before the current six-month agreement expires on June 9.
Despite confidence over the outcome, markets will be tense next week while negotiations continue in the Security Council, dealers said.
If the deal is signed, prices may not react immediately as the bureaucracy involved in signing new export contracts may delay fresh Iraqi oil shipments until later in June.
